analysis.one_liner: Extends wage, overtime, sick leave, break, contract, and anti-discrimination rights to the nation's roughly 2.2 million domestic workers.
analysis.headline: The Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act, covering an estimated 2.2 million workers, was introduced in July 2021, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given domestic workers — housekeepers, nannies, home care aides, and others — rights most workers already have: overtime pay for live-in workers, written contracts, paid sick days, meal and rest breaks, notice before schedule changes, and protection from retaliation and discrimination. It also set up a standards board, a reporting hotline, and extra Medicaid funding for home care. It was introduced in the Senate in July 2021, referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never moved again; Congress ended without the committee or the full Senate ever voting on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the roughly 2.2 million domestic workers in the U.S. — 9 out of 10 of them women, disproportionately people of color and immigrants, averaging about $12 an hour — would have gained overtime pay, paid sick days, breaks, written contracts, and protection from retaliation and discrimination. Families relying on home care would also benefit from a more stable, trained workforce [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nannies, housekeepers, and home care aides

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal exemption that has excluded live-in domestic workers from overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
Requires written contracts covering wages, hours, and duties for workers putting in 8 or more hours a week, and bans forced arbitration, non-disclosure, and non-compete clauses in those contracts.
Gives domestic workers earned paid sick time (1 hour per 30 worked, up to 56 hours a year), rest and meal breaks, and protection against wage deductions for cash shortages or breakage.
Requires employers of live-in workers to give written notice of termination plus 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance, and guarantees live-in workers access to phone and internet.
Extends Title VII anti-discrimination protections to domestic workers and bans retaliation, including threats to report a worker's immigration status.
Creates a Domestic Worker Wage and Standards Board, a national hotline, health-and-safety training grants, and a temporary increase in the federal Medicaid match to help fund home-care work.

analysis.who_pays: Household employers and agencies that hire domestic workers would bear the cost of overtime for live-in workers, severance or 30 days of lodging on termination, paid sick time, scheduling notices, and written contracts. Some of those costs could be passed on to middle-class families employing caregivers directly, and some care arrangements might become more formal or more expensive [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's requirements would fall heavily on private households, not just agencies: families employing a nanny or home health aide would need written contracts, scheduling notice of at least 72 hours, paid meal and rest breaks, and paid sick time accrual, and live-in employers would owe 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance on termination — real administrative and cost burdens for ordinary families, not just wealthy ones.

Employers of people with disabilities in shared living arrangements are carved out of the scheduling, break, and paid-sick-time rules, an acknowledgment that the bill's costs could otherwise fall on vulnerable care recipients, which signals the compliance burden was a genuine concern even to the bill's drafters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were substantial and targeted: about 2.2 million low-paid workers, 9 out of 10 of them women and disproportionately people of color and immigrants, would have gained enforceable wage, break, sick-leave, and anti-retaliation rights [S3]. The costs fall on household employers (paperwork, scheduling rules, paid breaks) and on home-care agencies and platforms that would absorb overtime and compliance costs, some of which could be passed on to families paying for care or reduce informal care arrangements. The bill was broad and its compliance burden on ordinary households employing a single caregiver was real, but the core protections address documented, widespread wage theft and isolation in an industry where 91% of workers who faced problems did not complain for fear of losing their jobs [S3]. The chief weakness is procedural: it died in committee without amendment or hearing, so its practical workability was never tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the bill on July 29, 2021, joined by 11 original cosponsors and 15 total cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote. The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Household employers, care agencies, and labor-platform operators who would have faced new overtime, severance, sick leave, and contracting obligations; domestic workers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 original cosponsors.

for.name: 15 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; the chair never scheduled a markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the party's Senate majority status in the 50-50 chamber gave its members effective leverage to keep labor bills off the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced in a Senate where Democrats held exactly 50 seats.

industries.industry: Domestic workers (housekeepers, nannies, home care aides, caregivers)
industries.note: The bill would have extended overtime, sick leave, breaks, written contracts, anti-discrimination and anti-retaliation protections to a workforce of roughly 2.2 million that federal labor law has largely excluded [S3].

industries.industry: Household employers and domestic-work staffing and platform companies
industries.note: Families and agencies employing domestic workers would bear new costs: overtime for live-in staff, severance or lodging on termination, paid sick time, scheduling-notice rules, and written contracts [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Medicaid home- and community-based care providers
industries.note: The bill would have raised the federal Medicaid match for services provided by domestic workers, offsetting some higher labor costs for state-funded home care [S2, S3].
